headlines.title: Former Meta engineer says Instagram took a ‘don't ask, don't tell' approach on kids under 13
headlines.description: A former engineering director at Meta who has testified before Congress about child safety on Instagram told jurors Wednesday at a landmark trial that the company took a “don’t ask, don’t tell” approach on kids under 13 on its platforms. During his second day of testimony, Arturo Béjar said Meta consistently prioritized profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being. “If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said. The trial that began Tuesday in federal court in Oakland, California, pits Meta against the states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey and is expected to last about six weeks. The four states were among 29 that sued the tech giant in 2023 over child safety and privacy — the other 25 will go to trial later. The company also faces lawsuits in state courts, including one underway in Tennessee. The lawsuit accuses Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hide these harms from the public. It also argues that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent, in violation of federal law. Meta says users must be at least 13 years old to create an account, in line with the law, called the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA. “The attitude in particular on Instagram was ‘Don’t ask, don’t tell,’” Béjar said in response to a question about his perception of the company’s attitude towards users under 13. The company has rejected the claims and said evidence at the trial will show its commitment to safety. “You will hear over the course of this case a lot of important issues, issues like teen mental health, issues like social media, issues like how teens use social media,” Meta lawyer Paul Schmidt said Tuesday. “Those are important issues, and they’re issues where Meta believes that it has a responsibility. It has a responsibility to act on its own. It has a responsibility to try to work with teens and parents in partnership to try to address those questions.” Plaintiffs’ witness says safety was an ‘afterthought’ Béjar worked at Facebook from 2009 to 2015, attracting wide attention for his work to combat cyberbullying. He returned from 2019 to 2021 as a contractor to work on safety issues. He testified before Congress in 2023 about social media and the teen mental health crisis, saying that Meta executives, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, knew about harms Instagram was causing but chose not to make meaningful changes to address them. In his testimony Wednesday, Béjar said employee performance reviews and compensation for those who worked on user-facing products were mostly focused on user numbers and how long they spend with those products. “In that context, safety was an afterthought,” he said. The states are seeking changes to user experiences for Facebook and Instagram as well as financial damages, which could include billions of dollars in penalties. In a written statement, the office of California’s attorney general said if Meta loses, the amount of any damages would be set by the court. “This case is about stopping Meta from offering a dangerous product to teens, and from lying to teens, families, and the public about the dangerousness of their platforms. The primary remedy under our state consumer protection law is an injunction,” the statement said. Béjar walked through Meta features he said were designed for adults and are “inherently unsafe for teenagers.” This includes video autoplay, which can mean teens see videos that may cause them harm even if they don’t click on them; as well as various counters that track how many people liked, viewed or commented on your content or how many followers you have. Child development experts have noted teenagers are more susceptible to social comparison than adults, so products that reward popularity can be more harmful to their mental health. Age verification has been criticized for not going far enough Despite Meta’s statements that it works to find kids under 13 on its platforms and ban them, Béjar testified that he found “tens of thousands” of kids under 13 on Instagram through his research. He said it was “common knowledge” at the company that such young children were on Instagram. “Meta has one of the most sophisticated infrastructures in the world to detect fake accounts,” he said. But despite that, he added, there were “no goals, no metrics” to detect and check kids’ ages who were suspected to be under 13. Over the years, Meta has introduced features it says are designed to make the experience safer for young people. But Béjar said these did not work. For instance, a tool called “Take a Break,” introduced in 2021, is a feature that is “designed to fail,” he said. First, it is a setting that people have to turn on if they want to use it. Béjar said that in his experience building settings, very few users actually go through the trouble of turning them on. He compared it to an airbag that drivers have to turn on every time they get in a car. “A safety tool has to be on by default,” he said. The feature can also be dismissed with a tap of a finger. If Meta was serious about wanting users to take a break, Béjar said, it would not be so easily swiped away. ___ AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story from Los Angeles.

headlines.title: Wahab narrowly ahead of Hernandez in California Congressional District 14 race
headlines.description: State Sen. Aisha Wahab, D-Hayward, was narrowly leading in the early results released from Tuesday’s special election to fill the rest of the congressional term in the East Bay seat formerly represented by Eric Swalwell. Wahab had 33,399 votes, or 51%, compared to 32,043 and 49% for Melissa Hernandez, a BART board director and former Dublin mayor, according to the unofficial results released from the initial vote-by-mail ballots counted by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters. The two were in a runoff to fill the rest of Swalwell’s term that ends in January for California’s 14th Congressional District after neither garnered a majority in a June 16 special election where Wahab received 43% of the vote and Hernandez 17%. Swalwell resigned from his congressional seat in April amid accusations of sexual assault. He has denied all allegations against him. The county Registrar of Voters said more results from the election will be released on Friday, then again Aug. 26 and Aug. 28. Along with Tuesday’s election to decide who fills the seat for the final months of Swalwell’s term, Wahab and Hernandez finished as the top two candidates in the June 2 primary and will face off again in November in a separate runoff for the next congressional two-year term to represent District 14, which includes the cities of Hayward, Pleasanton, Livermore, Union City, Castro Valley, and parts of Dublin and Fremont. Decision 2026 Aug 18 Decision 2026 Aug 17 California special election to fill Swalwell's Congressional District 14 seat

headlines.title: Arrest made in suspected Richmond arson that killed man, 5-year-old boy
headlines.description: A man was arrested on suspicion of murder and arson after a Richmond house fire killed a 47-year-old man and 5-year-old boy, police said, adding a woman and child were also critically hurt in the blaze. Firefighters initially responded to a one-alarm fire on the 200 block of 15th Street at about 8:08 p.m. Tuesday. The fire was declared under control just before 9 p.m., and its cause remains under investigation. About 45 minutes after the initial response, while crews were mopping up the first fire, they noticed smoke and flames coming from a home two doors north. The second fire was upgraded to three alarms due to its significant size and the resources needed to respond to the number of victims, fire officials said. Richmond firefighters were assisted by crews from the El Cerrito Fire Department and Contra Costa County Fire Protection District. Firefighters entered the second home and found four people inside. All four were rescued and taken to a hospital, officials said. The 47-year-old man and 5-year-old boy died as a result of the fire, while a 33-year-old woman and 2-year-old girl remained in critical condition. No one was injured in the first fire. Authorities said the two fires were not related. Detectives with the Richmond Police Department’s homicide unit began investigating after the second fire started. During the investigation, detectives identified 32-year-old Sergio Rivera-Vega as the person suspected of intentionally setting the second home on fire, police said. Rivera-Vega is a relative of the victims and lived at the home. Police said Rivera-Vega was found near the scene and taken into custody without incident. Rivera-Vega was booked into jail on two counts of murder and two counts of arson causing great bodily injury, according to police. His bail was set at $2.5 million. Because both fires are considered suspicious, arson investigators, along with the Richmond Police Department and the Contra Costa County Sheriff’s Office, are investigating.

headlines.title: Dog rescued as fire damages 2 San Jose homes
headlines.description: Firefighters responded to a second-alarm residential fire involving two homes in San Jose on Wednesday, according to the San Jose Fire Department. The fire was reported on the 2000 block of Santiago Avenue. Fire officials said both homes had compromised gas meters that were fueling the flames. PG&E crews secured the gas lines, according to the fire department. Firefighters rescued one dog, and no injuries were reported. Authorities asked people to avoid the area while crews responded to the fire.

headlines.title: 9-year-old boy taken to trauma center after being hit by driver in Santa Rosa
headlines.description: A driver struck a 9-year-old boy as he was crossing a street in Santa Rosa Tuesday night, leaving him with significant injuries, police said. The collision happened at about 8:30 p.m. along the 900 block of Yulupa Avenue, according to police. The child was crossing Yulupa Avenue when he was hit by a 41-year-old Santa Rosa man driving a white Ford Mustang, police said. Investigators believe the boy was in a marked crosswalk when he was struck. They were working to determine if the crosswalk lights were activated at the time. The boy suffered significant injuries and was taken to a regional trauma center by ambulance, police said. The driver stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. Alcohol and drugs do not appear to have played a role in the collision. It wasn’t immediately known how fast the driver was going at the time. An investigation is underway. Anyone who witnessed the collision or has additional information is asked to email police investigator Anthony Matteri at amatteri@srcity.org.

headlines.title: Foul play suspected in Chantel Brooks' disappearance, Fairfield police say
headlines.description: Foul play may have been involved in the disappearance of Chantel Brooks, the Fairfield Police Department said in a statement Tuesday. Brooks, who turned 37 last week, was last seen on July 17 at 1:45 a.m. leaving a CVS Pharmacy store in the 300 block of East Travis Boulevard in Fairfield, where she lives. Security camera footage from Le Nain Hotel in San Francisco’s Tenderloin District, where Brooks is a desk clerk, shows her leaving work at around 12:20 a.m. that night. On August 5, Fairfield Police issued a public notice of Brooks’ disappearance and requested the family’s help. Her brothers, Kevin Robinson and Omar Hasan, said in an interview that they’ve been meeting every week with Fairfield police for updates on the case. Hasan, who lives in Reno, Nevada, has been staying with family in Vallejo during the search. “When we first heard about it, we hit the ground running,” Robinson said. “Being her brothers, we’re her first line of protection … We’re all on our knees together, praying.” Brooks, who was born and raised in San Francisco, has 13 brothers and sisters, Robinson said, as well as cousins all around the Bay Area. “Any time we get a tip, we all know about it,” said Robinson, noting that he and his siblings are communicating more than they have in years. Family members have gone door-to-door in Fairfield to ask about Brooks and learn more about her life in Fairfield. They celebrated her 37th birthday with a vigil on Thursday in Fillmore-Turk Mini Park in San Francisco, said Robinson. “She’s warm and outgoing,” Robinson said. “Everyone she meets remembers her.” To date, the investigative efforts have included dozens of search warrants, multiple coordinated ground searches involving search and rescue resources through the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, as well as extensive aerial drone grid searches. The department is also working closely with the Solano County District Attorney’s Office while working through various leads in her disappearance. The public is urged to call the Fairfield Police Department at 707-428-7300 or email case267208@fairfield.ca.gov. Anonymous tips can be left with the department’s Investigations Division at 707-428-7600.

headlines.title: Oakland Unified receives negative credit rating outlook
headlines.description: There are new concerns about the financial health of the Oakland Unified School District after a Fitch credit rating gave the district a negative outlook for the current fiscal year. Fitch cited several factors, including ongoing fiscal pressure, the loss of unrestricted reserves and uncertainty over the district’s ability to restore fiscal stability. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the latest Fitch rating is one notch below the district’s previous grade. The assessment comes as district leaders have recently said OUSD’s finances have significantly improved, including reaching a balanced budget. Fitch and the Chronicle are both owned by Hearst. OUSD did not provide a response.

headlines.title: Death of Six Flags Discovery Kingdom dolphin prompts calls to relocate remaining animals
headlines.description: A bottlenose dolphin that spent more than four decades at Six Flags Discovery Kingdom in Vallejo was euthanized last month after years in captivity, prompting an animal rights group to renew calls for the park’s remaining dolphins to be moved to seaside sanctuaries. Chelsea was a bottlenose dolphin that was part of Six Flags Discovery Kingdom’s marine mammal program and was used in shows and visitor encounters. Chelsea’s life ended July 14. Her entry in the Marine Mammal Inventory Report, a federal record maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Marine Fisheries Service to track dolphins and other marine mammals held in captivity, lists her cause of death as euthanasia due to “multiple recurring chronic diseases” and a “declining quality of life.” This death has become the group’s most recent focus in their longstanding criticism of dolphins being held in captivity for entertainment. On Monday, PETA sent a letter to Six Flags Entertainment Corp. CEO John Reilly asking the company to end its swim-with-dolphins encounters and commit to moving the surviving dolphins at Discovery Kingdom to seaside sanctuaries. Such sanctuaries would allow the animals to live in larger, more natural environments while remaining under human care. Six Flags Discovery Kingdom did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Chelsea’s death or PETA’s calls for changes to the park’s dolphin program. PETA president Tracy Reiman said Chelsea spent more than 40 years confined to tanks and criticized the park for breeding and using dolphins in shows and visitor encounters. “For more than 40 years, Six Flags Discovery Kingdom sentenced Chelsea to a life of misery in a sad, shallow pool,” Reiman said in a statement. In its letter to Reilly, PETA pointed to Chelsea’s history as an example of why it believes Six Flags should move away from dolphin entertainment altogether. The organization said dolphins have complex social and physical needs that cannot be met in captivity and cited welfare concerns including stress, disease and abnormal behavior. The group placed Chelsea’s death in the context of a broader move away from captive dolphin attractions, noting in its letter that several major travel companies no longer sell tickets to venues offering dolphin encounters and that some countries have restricted or banned dolphin captivity. “Chelsea deserved a future beyond concrete tanks,” Reiman wrote in the letter. “It’s too late for her, but there’s still time to do the right thing for the surviving dolphins.

headlines.title: Man arrested on suspicion of vehicular manslaughter for pedestrian death in SF
headlines.description: A 50-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of vehicular manslaughter for a collision that killed a pedestrian last month in San Francisco’s South of Market neighborhood, police announced Wednesday. Isaac Bowler was arrested in connection with the collision that was reported shortly after 4 a.m. on July 14 in the 200 block of Sixth Street near Howard Street, according to San Francisco police. The pedestrian was taken to a hospital and succumbed to his injuries there, and was later identified by the city Medical Examiner’s Office as David Reinhart, a 57-year-old San Francisco resident. About a month later, investigators developed probable cause to arrest Bowler. He was arrested in San Francisco on Monday on suspicion of vehicular manslaughter, failing to exercise due care for a pedestrian, and failing to provide proof of insurance, police said. Police asked anyone with more information about the case to call their tip line at 415-575-4444 or to send a tip by text message to TIP411 with “SFPD” at the start of the message. The pedestrian advocacy nonprofit Walk San Francisco said the July 14 crash marked the second fatality in the area of Sixth and Howard streets in less than a year after a 78-year-old man was killed there on Aug. 10, 2025.

headlines.title: Former Meta employee testifies in high-profile social media trial
headlines.description: Day two of Meta’s high-profile trial in Oakland federal court is underway, with much of Wednesday morning focused on testimony from a former company employee turned whistleblower. At the center of the case are allegations that Meta misrepresented features on its apps and whether they are addictive. Arturo Bejar, a former Meta employee, testified about the company’s app design, particularly for younger users. Bejar claimed Meta’s apps are designed to keep users scrolling as a way to increase advertising revenue. When asked about Meta’s approach to users under 13, Bejar described it as “don’t ask, don’t tell.” He testified that underage users are relatively easy to identify. Videos shown in court depicted young users posting their ages while participating in online trends. Bejar also testified about a letter he wrote to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg before leaving the company in which he raised concerns about how the company addressed harmful experiences on its platforms. In the letter, Bejar said he believed there was a “critical gap” between Meta’s approach to harm and how users experienced it. He wrote that 51% of Instagram users reported having a harmful or bad experience within the previous seven days, but only 1% of those users reported the experience. Of those reports, he said, 2% resulted in the content being removed. Bejar appealed directly to Zuckerberg, saying he believed addressing the issues would require a cultural shift within the company. Meta’s attorneys began their cross-examination of Bejar on Wednesday, and questioning is continuing. The trial pits Meta against 29 states, including California, over allegations involving the company’s social media platforms and their potential risks to young users.

headlines.title: One of Santa Clara County's last fruit orchards faces closure
headlines.description: One of the last remaining fruit orchards in Santa Clara County may soon be uprooted to make way for housing, a sign of changing times for the region’s agricultural landscape. If Santa Clara County officials sign off on the plan, Andy’s Orchard in Morgan Hill will be sold and replaced with hundreds of homes, two parks and pickleball courts. Andy Mariani, 80, told NBC Bay Area’s Marianne Favro about his family’s decision to sell amid an uncertain future. His family purchased the orchard in 1957. Now, nearly 70 years later, the property holds about 7,000 trees, including his main crop of cherries. Mariani noted that when his family first moved to the area, they were surrounded by 30 other farms. But times have changed. “They’re gone. We’re the last ones,” Mariani said. Today, his more than 50-acre orchard is surrounded by million-dollar homes. Mariani said that urbanization has impacted his crops, though environmental shifts have dealt the heaviest blow. “The biggest problem is climate change,” Mariani said. “It warms the winter temperatures and cherries require a certain amount of winter cold, so this year we only got 5% of our crop and in fact, in the last 10 years, we have not made any money on cherries.” Mariani considers himself a “dirt farmer,” as he derives all of his income directly from the farm’s production. Even though his flavorful peaches, plums, and figs remain popular—with some even being sold to high-end New York restaurants—the once-profitable business is no longer sustainable. “You can’t continue to survive when you’re not producing fruit,” Mariani said. Greta and Bernd Liebelt of Morgan Hill have been visiting Andy’s store every week for more than 20 years. They said they are saddened to learn their trips now have an expiration date. “What’s unique about here is you don’t find fruit anywhere else that’s as good as Andy’s fruit,” Greta Liebelt said. “He’s ruined me for all grocery store fruits.” Bernd Liebelt said he is concerned that what is happening to the orchard is part of a growing trend across the state. “You’re seeing all kinds of building, and as a result, a lot of agriculture is going away and being replaced by housing,” he said. Mana Investments, a California real estate investment firm, now holds an option to buy the Mariani ranch. The firm plans to use the land to build 376 homes. Mariani said his country store will likely remain open until September of next year. He held out as long as he could. “It’s an end of an era,” Mariani said. “I feel bad, but if you can’t make it, it’s hard to justify being here.”

headlines.title: East Bay commute ranked among the worst in the US, study finds
headlines.description: The Bay Area — and California in general — has no shortage of challenging commutes, but a new study shows that the East Bay has one of the worst. The study asked more than 3,000 commuters across the nation one question: What’s the worst place to commute, and how much would you pay to avoid it? When all the answers and dollars were counted up, the MacArthur Maze, a large freeway interchange in Oakland, held a dubious distinction, with drivers who regularly navigate those roads saying they’d pay more than $3,000 a year to skip it. What makes the MacArthur Maze such a nightmare for commuters that they’d be willing to shell out that much money? Drivers tell NBC Bay Area it’s the sheer volume of traffic on the MacArthur Maze at all times of the day, which all comes together in one massive structure with multiple on-ramps and off-ramps. The formal name for the MacArthur Maze is the East Bay Distribution Structure, according to Caltrans. The roadways handle over 250,000 drivers per day, helping explain why it’s called “The Maze.” NBC Bay Area’s Thom Jensen has more in the video above.
